content.title: Random Sampling, Random Assignment, and Representativeness
content.overview: On the SAT Math test, evaluating the validity of statistical claims depends on the study design. This lesson focuses on how to ensure sample representativeness through random sampling and how to establish the basis for causal links in experiments through random assignment.
learning_objectives: Understand the definition of random sampling and its impact on the scope of generalization.
Understand the definition of random assignment and its role in experimental design.
Distinguish between the logic of sample representativeness and experimental intervention.
Determine whether a conclusion can be generalized to an entire population based on the study design.

sections.title: Random Sampling and Representativeness
sections.content: Random sampling refers to the process of randomly selecting individuals from a population to form a sample. Its core purpose is to ensure representativeness, meaning the characteristics of the sample reflect the characteristics of the population. If a sample is randomly selected, the study's conclusions can generally be generalized to the entire population from which the sample was drawn. If it is not a random sample (e.g., convenience sampling or voluntary participation), the conclusions apply only to that specific sample and cannot be generalized.

sections.title: Random Assignment and Experimental Control
sections.content: Random assignment refers to the process of randomly assigning individuals participating in a study to either an experimental group (receiving the intervention) or a control group (not receiving the intervention). The purpose of random assignment is to ensure that the two groups are essentially identical in all known and unknown characteristics before the experiment begins. This is a prerequisite for inferring cause-and-effect because it eliminates confounding factors caused by individual differences.

sections.title: Comparison of Sampling and Assignment
sections.content:
Random sampling determines 'to whom' the conclusion applies (scope of generalization), while random assignment determines 'whether the intervention caused the result' (causal inference). In SAT problems, if a study uses random sampling but not random assignment, it is typically an observational study and can only yield correlational conclusions; if random assignment is used, it is typically an experiment and can explore causal relationships.

![Statistical Study Design Process](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/d6861f69-71b7-4b8b-a1c6-b30fd2bebd4f-1786502085565-43.webp)

worked_examples.question: A city's department of education wants to understand the satisfaction of high school students citywide regarding a new lunch program. They randomly selected 500 students from 30 high schools across the city for a survey. The results showed that 80% of the students were satisfied. To which group is this study's conclusion most appropriate to generalize?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the sampling method. The problem explicitly states 'randomly selected.' Step 2: Determine the sampled population. The sample was drawn from 'high school students citywide.' Step 3: Draw the conclusion. Because random sampling was used, the conclusion can be generalized to all high school students in the city. Note that it cannot be generalized to middle school students or all citizens in the city, as they were not in the sampled population.

worked_examples.question: Researchers recruited 100 volunteers to test a new memory method. They randomly assigned the volunteers into two groups: Group A learned the new method, and Group B used a traditional method. The results showed that Group A's test scores were significantly higher than Group B's. Which of the following statements does this study design best support?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the assignment method. The problem states volunteers were 'randomly assigned into two groups.' Step 2: Analyze representativeness. Since the participants were 'volunteers' rather than a random sample, the scope of generalization is limited. Step 3: Analyze causality. Because random assignment was used, the study can support a causal conclusion that 'the new memory method caused the increase in scores.' Therefore, the conclusion is: For this group of volunteers, the new memory method is the cause of the score improvement.

common_mistakes: Confusing random sampling with random assignment: Assuming that the word 'random' alone allows generalization to everyone.
Overgeneralization: Generalizing conclusions from a random sample of a specific group (e.g., athletes) to all humans.

Ignoring volunteer bias: Volunteer samples are usually not representative; even if random assignment is performed within the experiment, the conclusions are difficult to generalize to the general public.
exam_tips: When you see 'Randomly selected,' immediately think of 'Generalizable.'
When you see 'Randomly assigned,' immediately think of 'Cause-and-effect.'
If the sample was not randomly selected, the conclusion must be limited to the sample itself or a group with characteristics highly similar to the sample.
content.recap: Random sampling ensures the sample represents the population, allowing for generalization; random assignment ensures balance between groups, allowing for causal inference. When evaluating statistical claims, you must distinguish the functions of these two processes.

knowledge_claims.content: Random sampling is a process where every member of a population has an equal chance of being selected for the sample.
If a study uses random sampling, its results can generally be generalized to the entire population that was sampled.
Random assignment is the process of randomly assigning study subjects to different treatment groups, such as an experimental group and a control group.
The primary purpose of random assignment is to support cause-and-effect inferences by balancing differences between groups.
Random sampling determines the scope of application for the conclusion (who), while random assignment determines the nature of the conclusion (causality).
If a sample is based on voluntary participation rather than random sampling, the conclusion cannot be reliably generalized to a broader population.
In the absence of random assignment, a causal conclusion cannot be drawn even if a correlation between two variables is observed.
When evaluating the generalizability of a conclusion, one should check if the sample source is consistent with the target population and was randomly selected.
For a random sample containing only a specific profession (e.g., doctors), the conclusion cannot be generalized to other professional groups.
Using both random sampling and random assignment in an experimental design is the strongest way to obtain conclusions that are both representative and causally explanatory.

items.stem: Residents of a town were surveyed to determine whether they are satisfied with the concession stand at the local park. A random sample of 200 residents was selected. All 200 responded, and 87% said they are satisfied. Based on this information, which of the following statements must be true? I. Of all the town residents, 87% would say they are satisfied with the concession stand at the local park. Il. If another random sample of 200 residents were surveyed, 87% would say they are satisfied.
items.explanation: The correct answer is A: Neither. Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.

items.stem: For a baobab tree habitat in South Africa, a scientist randomly selected 50 baobab trees that were 17 years old and randomly assigned them to two groups. Each group was subjected to a different watering pattern for 2 consecutive years to observe whether the watering pattern affects the trees' growth rate. Based on the design of the study, what is the largest group to which these results can be applied?

options.A: All the 50 baobab trees that were selected in this habitat
options.B: All the baobab trees that were 19 years old in this habitat
options.C: All the baobab trees that were 17 years old in South Africa
options.D: All the baobab trees that were 17 years old in this habitat

items.explanation: The correct answer is D: All the baobab trees that were 17 years old in this habitat. Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.
